title: Serving the earth
tomorrow: why did the Buddha walk toward the man everyone ran from?

cards: Mai's program took the class to sketch at a creek this morning. The light was perfect, and so was the plastic: bottles in the reeds, a bag snagged on a branch. She drew around it.
The Vinaya has a story about a tree. A monk, building himself a hut, starts cutting down a tree that a spirit lives in. The spirit begs him to stop.
He keeps cutting, and the blow strikes the spirit's child. The spirit goes to the Buddha.

teach.h: A RULE: DON'T DESTROY PLANT LIFE.
teach.b: The Buddha makes a rule: monks are not to destroy plant life.
The neighbors had already been grumbling that the monks harmed life with one sense, the plants themselves. Notice the shape of it.
Like the rains retreat at the start of these two weeks, the rule came from listening to others, here even to a tree.

The Dhammapada gives the same care a picture, in Max Müller's translation: "As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village."

teach.h: THE BEE LEAVES THE FLOWER WHOLE.
teach.b: Take what you need, and leave the flower whole.
That's the teaching behind why monks who keep the Vinaya don't cut living plants, why temples tend trees and gardens, and why Ông has spent years on one small bonsai, shaping it, never forcing it.

teach.h: TEN MINUTES WITH A TRASH BAG.
teach.b: In the Buddhist texts the earth isn't scenery for practice. It's full of lives, small and rooted.
Serving it is the bee's way: take lightly, leave things whole. For Mai at the creek, that might be ten minutes with a trash bag before the sketchbook comes out.

how: Monks who keep the Vinaya avoid cutting living plants or digging the earth; Buddhist temples tend trees and gardens, and lay Buddhists take up care for land, water and animals as part of not harming living beings.

o: a vow never to eat food grown in the ground
a temple fee paid to plant trees on holy days
caring for forests, rivers and creatures as lives

games.q: the tree and the bee — tap the pairs.
p: takes nectar, leaves the flower whole

s: in the Buddhist texts, plants are just scenery for practice
the neighbors in the Vinaya story speak of plants as life with one sense, and the rule protects them.
the Vinaya forbids monks to destroy plant life
the rule came after a monk cut a tree a spirit lived in.
the Dhammapada's bee damages the flower a little to get its nectar
in Max Müller's words, it departs "without injuring the flower".

games.q: your family's temple plans to release balloons at a festival, and a cousin says it's harmless fun. what fits the Vinaya's care?
o: suggest something that leaves no litter, like planting a tree together
go ahead; a festival's good intentions make up for a little trash
skip the festival entirely, since any celebration harms the earth
games.why: the bee takes what it needs and leaves the flower whole. a festival can do the same: celebrate, and leave the place unharmed.

practice: Find one living thing within reach: a houseplant, a leaf outside the window, a weed in a sidewalk crack. Look at it the way the bee visits the flower, closely, taking nothing: its color, its edges, how it turns toward the light.
Then let your eyes soften for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Serving the earth: the bee's way, taking what you need and leaving the flower whole.

orig.note: Pali: a bee; the image that opens Dhammapada 49.

carryVoice: Your line: the earth too. The Buddha's rule listened even to a tree. Twenty-three days, and the creek is waiting.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Suttavibhanga, Pacittiya 11 (destroying plant life; the monk of Alavi and the tree spirit)
